title: Derryloran & Cookstown
standfirst: The 1740 return records four Glasgow households in Derryloran; a 1766 return shows a larger local presence. Neither return says which later Cookstown family belonged to which house. Nineteenth-century records now distinguish John’s merchant son Benjamin from the Drapersfield mill family; neither is assigned to an earlier return household.
question: Can later Cookstown profiles be matched to a specific 1740 householder?
answer: The returns firmly establish a Glasgow population in Derryloran, but they give no ages, spouses, children or relationships. The later James and William profiles remain leads within the wider Tyrone setting, not identified 1740 householders.

chapters.title: Four same-name householders
body: The Protestant-householders return lists two James Glasgo and two William Glasgow or Glascy householders in Derryloran.
Repeated forenames make this a useful parish cluster, but do not distinguish fathers, sons, brothers or unrelated men.

chapters.title: A wider parish presence
body: The Derryloran religious return lists two James Glasgo and John at Drumearn, Samuel at Gortein, and William at Killycurry.
It records five definite households across three townlands, while leaving their identities and relationships unstated.

chapters.title: Later profiles remain unassigned
body: James of Corvanaghan, William of a reported Cookstown family, and the Mitchell-family reconstruction are geographically or chronologically relevant leads.
Corvanaghan is in Kildress, not Derryloran; no reviewed record maps any of these profiles to a named Derryloran return household.

chapters.title: A neighbouring Kildress delegate
body: The original Northern Star report names William Glasgow as a reform delegate at the 16 January Kildress meeting and as its subsequent chairman. William-2915 is old enough and geographically compatible, but the notice names no parents or wife.
Kildress is a neighbouring parish; this occurrence does not identify a Derryloran return householder.

chapters.title: John’s Benjamin and the Drapersfield partners
body: Benjamin-2059’s original 1856 marriage records him as a 20-year-old merchant of Cookstown and his father John as a merchant. This supports the existing father attachment; it does not identify John’s parents or specifically give Killycurragh as Benjamin’s residence.

The 1858 mill case names partners Benjamin and William, another William as their uncle, and the earlier Robert Glasgow and James Woods firm. Robert is father of the singular present plaintiff, without specifying which. A shared uncle does not by itself prove that the partners were brothers.

Benjamin Glasgow of Drapersfield granted land for the July 1870 gathering, after Benjamin-2059’s recorded February death. That current action strongly distinguishes the mill merchant from John’s son. William-3814, a retired bachelor merchant at Loy in 1883, is a strong candidate for the 1856 retirement notice and a possible uncle; the family link still needs a will or deed.
William-1675’s Ohio death notice gives age 55 rather than the attributed Mercury age 56. His 1855 death excludes him as the living 1858 uncle.

clusters.title: Derryloran return households
clusters.summary: The two returns establish repeated Glasgow household occurrences in the parish.
clusters.boundary: They name neither relationships nor a link to later profiles.

clusters.title: Cookstown and Kildress profile leads
clusters.summary: Three maintained profiles represent possible members of the wider Tyrone population.
clusters.boundary: No source identifies them with any 1740 Derryloran householder; Kildress must remain separate.

clusters.title: Cookstown merchant and mill families
clusters.place: Cookstown, Drapersfield and Loy, County Tyrone
clusters.status_label: Documented roles; family assignments under review
clusters.summary: The original records distinguish two Williams in the mill case and strongly separate the living Drapersfield Benjamin from Benjamin-2059.
clusters.boundary: No inspected record identifies John-2058’s parents or assigns a later merchant to a 1740 household.

links.label: No record assigns a later profile to a return household

proved: Four Derryloran Glasgow households occur in 1740.
Five Glasgow households occur in the 1766 Derryloran return.
Benjamin-2059’s 1856 marriage names his father John; both are merchants.
The 1858 mill case contains a co-plaintiff William and a distinct witness uncle William.
supported: The returns define a substantial local population worth following through later records.
The July 1870 Drapersfield Benjamin is strongly distinguished from Benjamin-2059, who died in February.
William-3814 is a strong compatible candidate for the 1856 retired merchant.
hypothesis: Later Cookstown reconstructions may belong to this wider Tyrone setting.
unresolved: Which named person, if any, was each 1740 or 1766 householder?
Which plaintiff was Robert Glasgow’s son, and who was their uncle William?
Who were John-2058’s parents? The mill notice does not answer this.

gaps.title: Follow each return householder
gaps.why: A lease, church, tax, probate or estate record could add relatives or continuity.

gaps.title: Inspect Cookstown family notes
gaps.why: They may test the reported Mitchell wife and son John.

gaps.title: Keep Kildress distinct
gaps.why: It prevents Corvanaghan from being silently treated as Derryloran evidence.

gaps.title: Identify the Drapersfield family
gaps.why: Mill deeds, 1842 proceedings or a retired merchant’s will could identify the two Williams and name the partner who was Robert’s son.
